Q2629730.t: An Arctic outpost where the Kolyma meets the ice
Q2629730.s: Where the wide, braided Kolyma finally reaches the East Siberian Sea, a small bay bites into the tundra: Ambarchik. In Soviet times ships sailing the Northern Sea Route anchored here to hand their cargo over to river boats heading upstream. Today the settlement is all but abandoned, surrounded by lake-speckled tundra and a sea that stays frozen for most of the year.
Q2629730.w: A small bay on the sea coast just east of the Kolyma's wide mouth, framed by flat tundra dotted with lakes.
f: The Kolyma, which meets the sea close by, flows for more than 2,100 km.
At almost 70° N, Ambarchik lies roughly 350 km north of the Arctic Circle.
The nearest town, Chersky, is about 100 km to the south.

q.q: Which river reaches the sea near Ambarchik?

Q212219.t: An empty Arctic island beside the continent's northern tip
Q212219.s: Mainland North America runs out just across the water from this island. Bellot Strait, about 2 km wide at its narrowest, separates Somerset Island from the tip of the Boothia Peninsula, the continent's northernmost point. The island is a bare, brownish plateau cut by steep valleys, with no permanent residents. In summer, belugas gather in Cunningham Inlet on its northern shore.
Q212219.w: A flat, brownish plateau between wide Barrow Strait to the north and the hair-thin Bellot Strait to the south.
f: Somerset Island covers about 24,800 km², yet nobody lives here permanently.
Bellot Strait is named after the French officer Joseph René Bellot, who joined the search for Franklin's lost expedition.
Fort Ross, a trading post at the island's southern tip, operated from 1937 until 1948.

q.q: Which strait separates Somerset Island from the mainland?

Q1044754.t: Green volcanic ridges and a lagoon strung with islets
Q1044754.s: The island is green right down to the water, and its eastern side is edged by one of the world's great lagoons: Marovo, a maze of turquoise channels and forested islets behind a double line of reef. Roviana Lagoon traces the south-western coast in much the same way. Inland, steep volcanic ridges carry unbroken rainforest, and clouds often snag on them.
Q1044754.w: A long green island with turquoise lagoons along its coasts; the round volcanic cone of Kolombangara rises just to the north-west.
f: Marovo Lagoon is often described as the largest saltwater lagoon in the world.
New Georgia covers about 2,000 km² and gives its name to a whole group of islands in the west of Solomon Islands.

q.q: Which huge lagoon lines New Georgia's eastern side?

Q913470.t: Flat coral tables afloat east of New Caledonia
Q913470.s: No mountains here: the Loyalty Islands are old coral reefs lifted out of the sea, so they look like flat green tables edged with pale cliffs and white sand. Lifou is the largest; Ouvéa is the showpiece, a thin crescent of land hugging a vast turquoise lagoon. Most islanders are Kanak, and each main island has its own language.
Q913470.w: A line of low, flat green islands east of New Caledonia's long, mountainous main island; Ouvéa's lagoon glows turquoise.
f: Lifou, the largest island of the group, covers more than 1,100 km².
Ouvéa's lagoon is lined by a white beach that runs for about 25 km.
These are uplifted atolls: their flat tops are old reef, raised out of the sea by movements of the Earth's crust.

q.q: Which is the largest of the Loyalty Islands?

Q274388.t: Coral specks and reef rings in the South China Sea
Q274388.s: Out in the open sea, scattered rings of pale reef and tiny coral islands break the deep blue: the Paracels. There are two main clusters, the Amphitrite Group in the north-east and the Crescent Group in the south-west, whose islets curve around a shallow lagoon. None of them rises much above the waves, and the largest, Woody Island, covers only about 2 km².
Q274388.w: Tiny pale islets and turquoise reef rings in open water, south-east of Hainan and east of central Vietnam.
f: The archipelago is made up of more than a hundred small coral islands, reefs and banks.
The Crescent Group owes its name to the arc its islets form around a lagoon.

q.q: In which sea do the Paracel Islands lie?

Q1720063.t: Namibia's wild north-west of red rock and dry rivers
Q1720063.s: This is one of the emptiest corners of southern Africa: a jumble of rust-red and ochre mountains cut by sandy riverbeds that carry water only after rare rains. To the west the land drops towards the fog-bound Skeleton Coast, and in the north the green thread of the Kunene River marks the border with Angola. Kaokoland is home to the Himba, semi-nomadic cattle herders.
Q1720063.w: Bare red-brown ranges and pale dry riverbeds, with Atlantic fog to the west and the Kunene's green ribbon to the north.
f: Himba women coat their skin and hair with otjize, a paste of butterfat and red ochre.
Desert-adapted elephants roam the region, following dry riverbeds in search of water and food.
On the Kunene, the Epupa Falls tumble through a belt of palm-fringed channels.

q.q: Which people live in Kaokoland?

Q193264.t: An island the size of Switzerland in the Amazon's mouth
Q193264.s: Before it reaches the Atlantic, the Amazon's brown water parts around an island almost as big as Switzerland. Marajó is really two landscapes: dense forest in the west and, in the east, flat grassland that floods in the rainy season and glitters with lakes. Its ranches are famous for water buffalo; in the town of Soure even the police have patrolled on them.
Q193264.w: A huge flat island between brown river channels, forest-dark in the west, pale and lake-spotted in the east.
f: At about 40,000 km², Marajó is often called the world's largest island formed between river and sea.
Long before Europeans, people here built earth mounds and made elaborate painted pottery now known as Marajoara.

q.q: Marajó is roughly the size of which country?

Q648391.t: An Arctic island named after a forgotten kettle
Q648391.s: In 1773 the merchant Ivan Lyakhov and his companions found a copper kettle on this island, left by visitors no one could name, and 'Kettle Island' it became. Kotelny is the largest of the New Siberian Islands: low hills, bare tundra and long snowbound months. To the south-east it merges with its neighbour Faddeyevsky through Bunge Land, a vast, almost bare sandy plain.
Q648391.w: A broad tundra island, white for most of the year; to the south-east, the pale, almost featureless sand flats of Bunge Land.
f: Kotelny alone covers about 11,700 km²; together with Bunge Land and Faddeyevsky, the landmass is roughly twice as big.
The New Siberian Islands were once famous for mammoth tusks, gathered here by ivory hunters.

q.q: Kotelny belongs to which archipelago?

Q21162.t: Pointed peaks and glaciers at the top of Europe
Q21162.s: The Dutch explorer Willem Barentsz named it in 1596 for what he saw: 'pointed mountains'. From the air it is exactly that, with sharp dark ridges, tongues of glacier spilling into fjords and snow almost everywhere. The main town, Longyearbyen, stands by Isfjorden, the long fjord that cuts deep into the west coast. In summer the sun does not set for four months.
Q21162.w: Jagged dark mountains between white glaciers, and long fjords, Isfjorden the largest, opening westward to the sea.
f: Spitsbergen covers about 37,600 km², more than Belgium.
About 2,500 people live in Longyearbyen, one of the northernmost towns in the world.
The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, dug into a mountainside near Longyearbyen, stores seeds from all over the world.

q.q: What does the name Spitsbergen mean?

Q134116.t: Where Parry's ships crossed 110° west and won a prize
Q134116.s: In 1819 William Edward Parry's two ships forced their way west through the ice and crossed 110° W off this island, winning his crews a £5,000 prize offered by Parliament. They then spent the winter frozen in at a bay they named Winter Harbour. Today Melville Island is uninhabited: brown, rolling, lake-dotted tundra where muskoxen and caribou graze.
Q134116.w: A large, low, brownish island on the north side of the wide Viscount Melville Sound, snow-covered most of the year.
f: At about 42,000 km², Melville Island is roughly the size of Denmark.
The boundary between the Northwest Territories and Nunavut crosses the island along 110° W.
Parry's men carved their names on a sandstone boulder at Winter Harbour, still known as Parry's Rock.

q.q: Who wintered at Melville Island in 1819–20?

Q207751.t: The island that half-closes the door to Hudson Bay
Q207751.s: Hudson Bay's northern entrance is half blocked by one big, flat island. Southampton is mostly a low limestone plain speckled with lakes, rising to hills only in the north-east, and sea ice surrounds it for much of the year. About a thousand people live in its only settlement, Coral Harbour, named for the fossil corals found nearby. Walruses, polar bears and huge colonies of snow geese share the rest.
Q207751.w: A large, flat, lake-speckled island across the northern mouth of Hudson Bay, often ringed by sea ice.
f: Covering about 41,000 km², Southampton is one of Canada's ten largest islands.
Most of Coral Harbour's roughly 1,000 residents are Inuit.

q.q: What is the only settlement on Southampton Island?

Q207925.t: An empty island on the Franklin expedition's route
Q207925.s: In 1846 John Franklin's Erebus and Terror sailed south down Peel Sound, the channel along this island's eastern shore, and never came home. Prince of Wales Island is still empty: a low, stony plateau scattered with countless lakes, frozen and snow-covered for most of the year. Summer turns it brown and blue, the lakes shining like shattered glass.
Q207925.w: A broad, low island between Somerset Island and Victoria Island, its surface freckled with countless lakes.
f: The island covers about 33,000 km² and has no permanent residents.
Peel Sound separates it from Somerset Island to the east; M'Clintock Channel separates it from Victoria Island to the west.

q.q: Which channel separates Prince of Wales Island from Somerset Island?

Q207666.t: Arctic ice caps and a forest that never turned to stone
Q207666.s: Ice caps crown the mountains and glaciers slide down into deep fiords, yet this was once warm forest. In the Geodetic Hills lie stumps of dawn redwoods about 45 million years old, so well preserved that the wood can still be cut and burned. The island is named after Axel Heiberg, a Norwegian businessman who helped fund Otto Sverdrup's expedition here around 1900.
Q207666.w: Mountains under white ice caps and glaciers reaching the sea, with Ellesmere Island to the east and the flat Ringnes islands to the west.
f: Axel Heiberg Island covers about 43,000 km² and has no permanent residents.
The neighbouring Ringnes islands are named after two brewer brothers who also sponsored Sverdrup.
A McGill University research station has studied the island's glaciers since the early 1960s.

q.q: What is preserved in Axel Heiberg's Geodetic Hills?

Q186841.t: The largest island on Earth with nobody living on it
Q186841.s: Scientists come here to rehearse for Mars. The Haughton crater, about 20 km across and blasted out by a meteorite millions of years ago, lies in a bare, rusty-grey polar desert that looks remarkably like the Red Planet. The eastern part of Devon Island is buried under a thick ice cap. At about 55,000 km², it is the largest island in the world with no permanent residents.
Q186841.w: A huge island north of Lancaster Sound: a white ice cap in the east, a bare brown plateau cut by canyons in the west.
f: Since the late 1990s the Haughton-Mars Project has used the crater to test equipment and methods for exploring Mars.
The Devon Ice Cap covers about 14,000 km² in the east of the island.

q.q: Which record does Devon Island hold?

Q148839.t: Remote volcanic islands where La Pérouse vanished
Q148839.s: The lost French expedition of La Pérouse ended here: in 1788 both its ships were wrecked on the reefs of Vanikoro, and the mystery was solved only nearly forty years later. The Santa Cruz Islands are the far eastern outpost of Solomon Islands, green and reef-fringed, with Nendö the largest. To the north, the near-perfect cone of Tinakula volcano rises straight out of the sea.
Q148839.w: Scattered green islands in coral reefs; the lone, sometimes steaming cone of Tinakula stands north of the largest island, Nendö.
f: In 1595 the Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña tried to found a colony on Nendö and died there that same year.
The islands were known for feather money: long coils made from the red feathers of a small honeyeater.

q.q: Whose expedition was wrecked on Vanikoro in 1788?

Q271674.t: Eight lonely atolls inside a giant marine reserve
Q271674.s: Eight atolls and reef islands are scattered across the central Pacific here, and almost nobody lives on them: only Kanton has a small community. The ocean around them is protected. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area covers about 400,000 km², roughly the size of California, and has been a World Heritage site since 2010. Its seldom-visited reefs are full of fish, sharks and seabirds.
Q271674.w: Tiny pale rings of reef with bright lagoons, far apart in deep blue ocean just south of the equator.
f: Kanton, the only inhabited island, is home to just a few dozen people.
The group lies just south of the equator, roughly midway between Hawaii and Fiji.

q.q: Which is the only inhabited Phoenix Island?

Q153732.t: Green islands beside the deepest trench on Earth
Q153732.s: Just offshore, the ocean floor drops into the Mariana Trench, which curves along the islands and reaches nearly 11 km at the Challenger Deep, about as deep as you are flying high. The islands form an arc some 800 km long: bigger, flatter Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan in the south, steep volcanic cones in the north. Magellan's expedition reached them in 1521.
Q153732.w: A north–south chain of green islands; the big ones, Guam, Saipan and Tinian, in the south, small volcanic cones to the north.
f: They are named after Mariana of Austria, the Spanish queen, in whose honour Jesuit missionaries renamed them in 1668.
Magellan's crew had called them the Islands of Thieves, Islas de los Ladrones.

q.q: Which expedition reached the Mariana Islands in 1521?

Q504043.t: Volcanic peaks inside one vast turquoise lagoon
Q504043.s: Picture Bora Bora on a larger scale: a ring of reef encloses a wide lagoon, and inside it rise the steep green remains of an old volcano. The largest island, Mangareva, climbs to about 440 m at Mount Duff. The Gambiers mark the south-eastern end of French Polynesia, and their lagoon farms are known for black pearls.
Q504043.w: A turquoise lagoon inside a thin ring of reef, with a cluster of steep dark-green islands within it.
f: About 1,500 people live in the Gambier Islands, most of them on Mangareva.
In 1797 the captain of the missionary ship Duff named the islands after the British admiral James Gambier.

q.q: Which is the largest of the Gambier Islands?

Q172697.t: Wild volcanic spires with no reef to soften them
Q172697.s: Unlike most of Polynesia, the Marquesas have almost no coral reefs or lagoons: the ocean hits the cliffs head-on, and green ridges and basalt spires shoot up from deep blue water. Tahiti is about 1,400 km away, and these are among the most remote islands on the planet. In 2024 the archipelago, with its seabird cliffs and ancient stone platforms, became a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Q172697.w: Steep dark-green islands with jagged ridges and no lagoons around them; surf breaks straight onto the cliffs.
f: The Spanish navigator Mendaña named them in 1595 after the Marquis of Cañete, viceroy of Peru.
Marquesan tattoo is among the most elaborate in Polynesia, sometimes covering the whole body.

q.q: What do the Marquesas lack that most Polynesian islands have?

Q38095.t: Darwin's islands of black lava and giant tortoises
Q38095.s: Dark lava fields, shield volcanoes with calderas like sunken bowls, and patches of green in the highlands: the Galápagos sit on the equator nearly 1,000 km off the coast of Ecuador. Charles Darwin spent about five weeks here in 1835, and the islands' finches, tortoises and iguanas later fed his thinking on evolution. Isabela, the largest island, is shaped a little like a seahorse.
Q38095.w: Dark volcanic islands with round calderas; the largest, Isabela, is a long, seahorse-shaped chain of volcanoes on the western side.
f: 'Galápago' is an old Spanish word for tortoise, after the giant tortoises that live here.
In 1978 the Galápagos were among the first twelve places inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage sites.
Marine iguanas, found only here, dive into the sea to graze on algae.

q.q: Who visited the Galápagos aboard HMS Beagle in 1835?

Q162126.t: Volcanic islands where tomorrow is next door
Q162126.s: The chain runs west to east as a line of green volcanic islands: big Savai'i and Upolu first, then Tutuila and the tiny Manu'a group. They are shared by Samoa and American Samoa, whose capitals are little more than 100 km apart yet a calendar day apart, because in 2011 Samoa moved to the other side of the International Date Line. Coral reefs draw pale borders around the dark-green shores.
Q162126.w: A west–east line of dark-green volcanic islands with pale reef edges; the two largest, Savai'i and Upolu, lie at the western end.
f: Samoa skipped 30 December 2011 entirely when it moved west of the International Date Line.
Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years on Upolu and is buried on Mount Vaea above Apia.
Fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way of life, is built around the extended family and its chiefs.

q.q: Which date did Samoa skip in 2011?

Q913624.t: Forested islands between a deep sea and a shallow one
Q913624.s: A long, low, forested island leads the group: Yamdena, with smaller islands scattered around it, set between the deep Banda Sea and the shallow Arafura Sea. This is a quiet corner of eastern Indonesia, far from the tourist trail. Its forests shelter the Tanimbar corella, a small white cockatoo that lives in the wild nowhere else, and villages still weave richly patterned ikat cloth.
Q913624.w: A long green island, Yamdena, running roughly north-east to south-west, with smaller islands and pale reef edges around it.
f: The main town, Saumlaki, lies at the southern end of Yamdena.
North of the islands the Weber Deep in the Banda Sea plunges more than 7 km.

q.q: Between which two seas do the Tanimbar Islands lie?

Q1980628.t: Volcanic islands in the gap between Luzon and Taiwan
Q1980628.s: North of Luzon, the strait between the Philippines and Taiwan is dotted with a loose cluster of volcanic islands: Calayan, Camiguin, Dalupiri, Fuga and Babuyan itself. Several peaks here are active volcanoes, and the cone of Babuyan Claro stands out from far away. In late winter and spring, humpback whales come to these warm waters to breed.
Q1980628.w: A scatter of green islands in open sea north of Luzon, several topped by volcanic cones; the Batanes lie farther north.
f: The Calayan rail, a flightless bird found only on Calayan island, was first described by scientists in 2004.
The islands belong to the Philippine province of Cagayan, on the northern tip of Luzon.

q.q: Which flightless bird was discovered in the Babuyan Islands in 2004?

Q171132.t: Dry, sunlit islands circling sacred Delos
Q171132.s: Scattered across the deep blue Aegean, the Cyclades are brown, bare and sharp-edged, each fringed with a thin white line of surf. Their name comes from the Greek word for a circle: the ancients saw them ringing the sacred island of Delos. At the southern end lies Santorini's broken ring, the drowned crater of a volcano; Naxos, the largest island, sits near the centre.
Q171132.w: Dozens of brown, bare islands in deep blue sea; in the south, the ring of cliffs of Santorini around a flooded caldera.
f: The group counts about 220 islands and islets.
Bronze Age islanders carved strikingly simple marble figures, now known as Cycladic figurines.
The Venus de Milo was found in 1820 on Milos, one of the Cyclades.

q.q: Which sacred island do the Cyclades 'circle'?

Q4991540.t: The 'endless plains' of the great migration
Q4991540.s: The Maasai name means 'endless plains', and from the air that is exactly what you see: golden or green grassland to the horizon, broken by dots of acacia and piles of granite boulders called kopjes. More than a million wildebeest, with zebras and gazelles, circle through it every year, following the rains. The highlands and the great crater of Ngorongoro rise at its south-eastern edge.
Q4991540.w: Vast flat grassland, tawny or green, with scattered trees and granite outcrops; Lake Victoria to the west, crater highlands to the south-east.
f: Serengeti National Park covers about 14,750 km² and has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981.
In the north the plains continue across the border into Kenya as the Maasai Mara.

q.q: What does the name Serengeti mean in the Maasai language?

Q83857.t: Central Europe's great flat bowl of fields and puszta
Q83857.s: The Tisza once flooded this plain every spring; today it is a flat chessboard of fields, its rivers tamed behind embankments and old meanders left behind as curved oxbow lakes. The plain fills about half of Hungary and spills into neighbouring countries. In the Hortobágy the open grassland, the puszta, survives, with grey cattle and spiral-horned sheep grazing to the horizon.
Q83857.w: A perfectly flat patchwork of fields, crossed by the winding Tisza and its crescent-shaped oxbow lakes.
f: Hortobágy, Hungary's first national park, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
On hot summer days the puszta is known for mirages, called délibáb in Hungarian.
Hungary's lowest point, about 78 m above sea level, lies on the plain near Szeged.

q.q: Which river winds across the Great Hungarian Plain?

Q1052758.t: A vast table of land dotted with green circles
Q1052758.s: Flat as a table and just as sharply edged, the Llano Estacado ends in steep escarpments, the Caprock in the east, that drop to lower country all around. On top the land is so level that roads run ruler-straight for tens of kilometres. The dominant pattern is green and brown circles: fields watered by pivot sprinklers that draw on the Ogallala Aquifer.
Q1052758.w: A flat plateau chequered with round irrigated fields, its eastern edge frayed by the Caprock Escarpment and Palo Duro Canyon.
f: Covering roughly 97,000 km², it is one of the largest tablelands in North America.
Coronado's expedition crossed it in 1541; he wrote that there were no landmarks at all, as if they were at sea.
Lubbock and Amarillo are the largest cities on the plateau.

q.q: Which aquifer waters the Llano Estacado's round fields?

Q26787455.t: A green oval cradled between snowy ranges
Q26787455.s: Walled in by the Pir Panjal range to the south-west and the Great Himalaya to the north-east, the valley floor lies about 1,600 m up and is strikingly flat and green. The Jhelum River meanders through it, feeding lakes such as Dal, beside Srinagar, and the broad Wular. Mughal emperors laid out terraced gardens here and came to escape the summer heat of the plains.
Q26787455.w: A flat oval valley, green in summer, ringed by snowy ranges; lakes glint around Srinagar in the middle.
f: The valley is roughly 135 km long and about 30 km wide.
Saffron is grown on the terraces around Pampore, south-east of Srinagar.
Wular Lake, fed by the Jhelum, is one of the largest freshwater lakes in South Asia.

q.q: Which river flows through the Kashmir Valley?

Q18677875.t: Hedgerows, chalk cliffs and the land of the Northmen
Q18677875.s: Normandy takes its name from the Northmen, Viking settlers granted this land in 911; their descendant William sailed from here to conquer England in 1066. From the air the countryside is a fine green mesh of small fields bounded by hedgerows, the bocage. White chalk cliffs line the coast north of the Seine estuary, and at the western end Mont-Saint-Michel rises from its tidal bay.
Q18677875.w: A patchwork of small green fields and hedges, with the wide Seine estuary to the east and the English Channel along the north.
f: Normandy's apple orchards give cider and Calvados, an apple brandy.
Tides in the Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel can rise and fall by more than 10 m.
Camembert, Livarot and Pont-l'Évêque cheeses are all named after places in Normandy.

q.q: In which year were Viking settlers granted the land that became Normandy?

Q12130.t: A ragged granite prow thrust into the Atlantic
Q12130.s: Brittany juts into the Atlantic like the bow of a ship, and its coast is frayed into headlands, rocky islets and deep estuaries. Inland, small fields and woods make a green quilt. The westernmost department is called Finistère, 'the end of the land'. Breton, a Celtic language related to Welsh and Cornish, is still spoken and taught here.
Q12130.w: A broad peninsula pointing west into the ocean, its edges frayed into headlands, islands and inlets; the island-filled Gulf of Morbihan on the south coast.
f: Near Carnac, about 3,000 standing stones form long rows raised more than 5,000 years ago.
The Gulf of Morbihan is dotted with dozens of islands; its name means 'little sea' in Breton.

q.q: Which Celtic language is spoken in Brittany?

Q1370633.t: A maze of blue water and dark forest
Q1370633.s: Water and forest interlock so tightly here that it is hard to say which is the background: blue lakes full of islands, threaded by narrow straits and long gravel ridges left by the ice sheet. Saimaa, the largest lake system, sprawls across the south-east. In winter it all turns white, and the lakes show only as smooth, flat patches among the trees.
Q1370633.w: An endless labyrinth of island-studded lakes and dark green forest; long, narrow ridges cross the water in places.
f: Finland has around 188,000 lakes, and a great many of them lie in this region.
The Saimaa ringed seal, one of the rarest seals on Earth, lives only in Lake Saimaa.
Punkaharju is an esker, a gravel ridge laid down by a river under the ice sheet, and a road now runs along it between lakes.

q.q: Which rare seal lives only in Lake Saimaa?

Q6146133.t: A broad ice-free lowland beside the world's biggest fjord
Q6146133.s: Most of east Greenland is mountains and ice, which makes Jameson Land stand out: a broad, rolling, snow-patched lowland with hardly a glacier on it. It lies on the north side of Scoresby Sund, the largest fjord system in the world. The land is built of soft sedimentary rocks, and muskoxen graze its tundra. The airstrip at Constable Point serves the remote village of Ittoqqortoormiit.
Q6146133.w: A wide brownish lowland north of the mouth of Scoresby Sund, between the mountains of Liverpool Land and the ice-capped ranges inland.
f: William Scoresby Jr named it in 1822 after Robert Jameson, his geology professor in Edinburgh.
Scoresby Sund reaches about 350 km inland from the open sea.

q.q: Which huge fjord system lies beside Jameson Land?

Q1081204.t: China's tropical island on the South China Sea
Q1081204.s: Hainan is China's tropical south: a big, rounded island with forested mountains in the middle and a rim of rice paddies, rubber plantations and beaches. The narrow Qiongzhou Strait separates it from the mainland, and the capital, Haikou, sits on the north coast facing it. At the southern tip, Sanya's bays draw crowds seeking winter sun.
Q1081204.w: A large rounded island with green mountains in the south-centre and flatter farmland in the north, across a narrow strait from the mainland.
f: Wuzhi Shan, 'Five Finger Mountain', the island's highest peak, rises to more than 1,800 m.
The Qiongzhou Strait is only about 20–30 km wide.
The Li people, one of China's officially recognised ethnic groups, live mainly in Hainan's mountainous interior.

q.q: Which strait separates Hainan from mainland China?

Q248654.t: An island almost entirely under one great ice dome
Q248654.s: A single smooth dome of ice, the Academy of Sciences Ice Cap, hides most of Komsomolets; it is among the largest in Russia. Only a thin rim of bare, stony ground shows at its edges. At the northern tip, Cape Arktichesky is a traditional starting point for skiers heading to the North Pole, a little under 1,000 km away.
Q248654.w: The northernmost island of Severnaya Zemlya: a smooth white ice dome with sharp edges, surrounded by sea ice most of the year.
f: The ice cap covers about 5,600 km², most of the island's roughly 9,000 km².
Severnaya Zemlya was discovered only in 1913 and first mapped in 1930–32 by Georgy Ushakov and Nikolai Urvantsev.
The island's name honours the Komsomol, the Soviet youth organisation.

q.q: Which cape of Komsomolets is a starting point for North Pole treks?

Q650720.t: The island facing Eurasia's northernmost cape
Q650720.s: Across the Vilkitsky Strait from this island lies Cape Chelyuskin, the northernmost point of mainland Eurasia. Bolshevik is the southernmost of Severnaya Zemlya's big islands, and less of it is buried than on its neighbours: ice caps hold the high ground, while bare, stony tundra and deep valleys fill the rest. The strait between it and the mainland is icebound for much of the year.
Q650720.w: A large island north of the Taymyr Peninsula, ice caps on its heights and grey-brown tundra around them, across a wide strait from the mainland.
f: Bolshevik Island covers about 11,000 km².
The Vilkitsky Strait, named after the explorer who found these islands in 1913, is a key passage of the Northern Sea Route.

q.q: Which cape lies across the strait from Bolshevik Island?

Q217372.t: The biggest island of Severnaya Zemlya, crowned with ice
Q217372.s: Several ice caps crown this island, the largest in Severnaya Zemlya, and between them run bare, deeply cut valleys. In the 2010s the Vavilov Ice Cap on its western side suddenly began to slide fast into the Kara Sea, pushing out a broad lobe of ice that shows clearly in satellite images. The highest point of the whole archipelago, Mount Karpinsky, rises here to about 965 m.
Q217372.w: A large island in the middle of Severnaya Zemlya: several white ice domes separated by dark, bare valleys and fjords.
f: October Revolution Island covers about 14,000 km².
Its name, given in the early 1930s, commemorates the revolution of October 1917.

q.q: Which is the largest island of Severnaya Zemlya?

Q779867.t: Low specks of land lost in the Kara Sea ice
Q779867.s: For most of the year it is hard to tell these islands from the sea around them: both are white and flat. They are a small cluster of low, bare islets in the Kara Sea, only about 15 km across in all, with nobody living on them. The group is named after the Arctic Institute in Leningrad, whose scientists explored and mapped much of the Soviet Arctic.
Q779867.w: A few tiny, low islets in the open Kara Sea, grey-brown in brief summer, lost under snow and ice otherwise.
f: The islands lie at about 75° N, nearly 1,000 km north of the Arctic Circle.
The Arctic Institute, founded in 1920, still works in St Petersburg as the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute.

q.q: In which sea do the Arctic Institute Islands lie?

Q944346.t: A lonely dome of ice on the northern Kara Sea
Q944346.s: Imagine a white shield dropped on the sea: Schmidt Island is almost entirely covered by a smooth ice cap that reaches nearly to the shore. It stands alone in the Kara Sea off the north-west coast of Severnaya Zemlya, and nobody lives on it. The island was discovered in 1930 by an icebreaker expedition led by Otto Schmidt, and now bears his name.
Q944346.w: A small, lone white dome in the sea north-west of Severnaya Zemlya, hard to tell from the ice around it for most of the year.
f: The Schmidt Ice Cap covers about 385 km², most of the island.
In 1937 Otto Schmidt led the landing of the first drifting research station near the North Pole.

q.q: Who is Schmidt Island named after?

Q504449.t: A rain-soaked island of wooden churches and ghost ships
Q504449.s: Green, rolling and often under cloud, Chiloé lies just off the Chilean mainland across the narrow Chacao Channel. Its eastern side is a quilt of small farms and inlets facing an inner sea dotted with smaller islands; the Pacific side is wilder, with dense forest. Islanders built dozens of wooden churches, and their folklore tells of the Caleuche, a ghost ship that sails these waters.
Q504449.w: A large green island south-west of Puerto Montt: farmland and inlets on the east side, dark forest facing the open Pacific.
f: Sixteen of Chiloé's wooden churches together form a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Covering about 8,400 km², Chiloé is Chile's second-largest island after Tierra del Fuego.

q.q: Which ghost ship sails through the folklore of Chiloé?

Q185532.t: The 'mother island' of the Moluccas, steep and forested
Q185532.s: Seram is long and mountainous, its ridges clothed in rainforest and often lost in cloud. Local tradition calls it Nusa Ina, 'mother island', the place the peoples of the central Moluccas came from. Manusela National Park covers much of the centre, climbing towards Mount Binaiya at about 3,000 m, and the smaller island of Ambon lies just off Seram's south-western coast.
Q185532.w: A long island, over 300 km from east to west, with a steep green mountain spine; smaller Ambon lies off its south-western end.
f: The salmon-crested cockatoo, a large pink-tinged parrot, lives in the wild only on Seram and a few nearby islands.
Covering about 17,000 km², Seram is the second-largest island of the Moluccas after Halmahera.

q.q: What does Seram's local name, Nusa Ina, mean?

Q201398.t: A four-armed island ringed by clove volcanoes
Q201398.s: Halmahera looks like a smaller copy of Sulawesi: four mountainous arms reaching out around three deep bays. It is the largest island of the Moluccas, the original Spice Islands. Just off its west coast rise the neat volcanic cones of Ternate and Tidore, rival sultanates that grew rich on cloves. On the northern arm, Dukono volcano often trails a plume of ash.
Q201398.w: A K-shaped island with four long arms around deep bays; small round volcanic islands, Ternate and Tidore, line its western shore.
f: Wallace's standardwing, a bird of paradise, lives on Halmahera and a few nearby islands.
Alfred Russel Wallace's famous 1858 letter on natural selection was sent from Ternate, just off Halmahera.

q.q: Which spice made the sultanates beside Halmahera rich?

Q83067.t: A mountain island that legend says was once a crocodile
Q83067.s: A Timorese legend tells that the island is the body of a giant crocodile that turned to land, and its long, tapering outline does suggest one. Unlike its volcanic neighbours, Timor was pushed up by the collision of the Australian plate with the edge of Asia. Its mountains stay brown and dry for much of the year and turn green only in the rainy season.
Q83067.w: A long island running south-west to north-east, with rugged brown-green mountains along its spine and the Timor Sea to the south.
f: The name comes from 'timur', the Malay and Indonesian word for east.
The island is shared by Indonesia in the west and Timor-Leste in the east.
Mount Ramelau, the highest peak, rises to nearly 3,000 m.

q.q: What does the name Timor mean?

Q1061269.t: A long green blade between two seas
Q1061269.s: Palawan is a long, narrow blade of green, more than 400 km from end to end and rarely more than 40 km wide, with the South China Sea on one side and the Sulu Sea on the other. Its northern end breaks up into limestone islands around El Nido, sheer grey towers rising from turquoise water. Near Puerto Princesa, a river runs for kilometres through a cave before reaching the sea.
Q1061269.w: A long, thin, mountainous island running north-east to south-west, with scattered limestone islets off its northern tip.
f: The Puerto Princesa Underground River is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Tubbataha Reefs, out in the Sulu Sea south-east of the island, is another World Heritage site, famous for diving.

q.q: Which sea lies along Palawan's eastern side?

Q6497558.t: The island of the Chocolate Hills
Q6497558.s: In the middle of Bohol, more than a thousand grassy, rounded hills rise from the plain like upturned bowls, so regular they look almost man-made. In the dry season the grass turns brown and they become the famous Chocolate Hills. The island itself is a rough oval fringed with reefs, and Panglao, joined to it by bridges, draws divers with its white beaches.
Q6497558.w: An oval green island between Cebu and Mindanao; the Chocolate Hills make a stippled patch in its interior.
f: The Philippine tarsier, a tiny primate with enormous eyes, lives in Bohol's forests.
The Chocolate Hills are limestone mounds shaped by rain and erosion.

q.q: Why are Bohol's Chocolate Hills so called?
q.a: They turn brown in the dry season
x: Their soil is dark volcanic ash

Q212777.t: Sugar fields beneath a smoking volcano
Q212777.s: Negros is the Philippines' sugar island: its western plains are a patchwork of cane fields, bright green while growing and bare brown after the harvest. Above them rises Kanlaon, an active volcano about 2,400 m high and the tallest peak in the Visayas. A mountain spine runs down the island's length, dividing the broad sugar lands of the west from the narrower east coast.
Q212777.w: A long, boot-shaped island west of Cebu, with the volcanic cone of Kanlaon in its northern half and green fields on the west.
f: Negros is often called the 'Sugarbowl of the Philippines'.
The island is split between two provinces, Negros Occidental and Negros Oriental.

q.q: Which crop dominates the plains of Negros?

Q211377.t: Green hills, a slender strait and a Mass from 1521
Q211377.s: Leyte is ruggedly green, with a mountain backbone down its length and coastal plains planted with coconut palms and rice. At its north-eastern corner, the strait separating it from Samar narrows to a winding channel. Off the southern tip lies little Limasawa, where Magellan's crew celebrated the first Christian Mass in the Philippines in 1521.
Q211377.w: A green mountainous island east of Cebu, separated from Samar in the north-east by a thin, winding strait.
f: The San Juanico Bridge, more than 2 km long, spans the strait between Leyte and Samar.
Volcanic heat in Leyte's mountains feeds some of the country's largest geothermal power fields.

q.q: Which island does the San Juanico Bridge link to Leyte?

Q219737.t: A big, forested island facing the open Pacific
Q219737.s: Samar's eastern coast looks straight out over thousands of kilometres of open Pacific, and it is often the first land that ocean storms reach in the Philippines. Inside, low mountains are cloaked in one of the country's largest surviving lowland rainforests, riddled with rivers, gorges and caves. Tiny Homonhon, off its southern tip, is where Magellan first stepped ashore in the Philippines in 1521.
Q219737.w: A big, rugged green island north of Leyte, its eastern shore open to the Pacific, its interior forested and cut by rivers.
f: Samar covers about 13,400 km², making it the third-largest island in the Philippines.
Samar Island Natural Park protects the largest stretch of its forest.

q.q: Where did Magellan first land in the Philippines in 1521?

Q332359.t: A triangle of rice plains with Boracay off its tip
Q332359.s: Panay is almost a perfect triangle: a mountain range runs along its western side, and broad, bright-green rice plains spread east towards Iloilo. Just off the north-western corner lies little Boracay, a thin sliver of land with a dazzling white beach. Every January the town of Kalibo holds the Ati-Atihan, one of the oldest and liveliest festivals in the Philippines.
Q332359.w: A large triangular island in the central Philippines: mountains in the west, a flat green plain in the east, Boracay off the north-west tip.
f: The fortress-like church of Miag-ao, near Iloilo, is part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Boracay's White Beach runs for about 4 km.

q.q: Which beach island lies off Panay's north-western tip?

Q211800.t: Home of the tamaraw, a buffalo found nowhere else
Q211800.s: South of Luzon, Mindoro's mountainous interior climbs to Mount Halcon at around 2,600 m and is often wrapped in cloud. The forests and grasslands of those mountains are the last refuge of the tamaraw, a small, stocky wild buffalo that lives only here. The island's Mangyan peoples still write in old Indic-derived scripts, carving verses into bamboo.
Q211800.w: A large, compact island south of Luzon across the Verde Island Passage, with forested mountains in its centre.
f: The Verde Island Passage off Mindoro's north coast is among the world's richest waters for marine life.
Apo Reef, off the west coast, is one of the largest coral reef systems in the Philippines.

q.q: Which wild animal lives only on Mindoro?

Q644636.t: The copper island with a long, thin panhandle
Q644636.s: Cyprus has an unmistakable outline: a broad body with a long, thin 'panhandle', the Karpas Peninsula, pointing north-east towards the Levant. In the west, the dark, pine-covered Troodos Mountains rise to about 1,950 m; a sharp limestone ridge runs along the north coast, and the flat Mesaoria plain fills the gap between. In winter, the salt lakes near Larnaca and Limassol fill with flamingos.
Q644636.w: A large island with a long, narrow peninsula pointing north-east; dark mountains in the west, a flat, pale plain in the middle.
f: The Latin word for copper, cuprum, comes from the island's name; its copper mines were famous in antiquity.
Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia.
Legend places the birth of Aphrodite at a sea rock off the south-west coast.

q.q: Which metal takes its Latin name from Cyprus?

Q200226.t: Muskox country at the western edge of the Arctic islands
Q200226.s: Flat to gently rolling tundra, laced with rivers and lakes, Banks Island faces the Beaufort Sea across its western shore. It is muskox country and has long held one of the largest herds of these shaggy animals in the world. The only village, Sachs Harbour, has around a hundred residents. In the north, Aulavik National Park protects the valley of the Thomsen River.
Q200226.w: A big, flat, brownish island at the western end of the Arctic archipelago, facing the Beaufort Sea, with lakes and river valleys scattered across it.
f: At about 70,000 km², Banks is Canada's fifth-largest island.
In 2006 a hunter near Sachs Harbour took the first confirmed wild grizzly–polar bear hybrid.

q.q: What is the only village on Banks Island?

Q27508031.t: Land of wood and water, under blue-hazed mountains
Q27508031.s: The Taíno called it Xaymaca, 'land of wood and water', and from the air the name fits: green forest, rivers and a white-edged coast. In the east, the Blue Mountains rise to about 2,250 m, often veiled in a bluish haze. In the west-centre lies Cockpit Country, a limestone landscape pitted with steep hollows that make it look like an egg carton.
Q27508031.w: An oval green island south of Cuba; the high Blue Mountains in the east, a curving sand spit enclosing Kingston's harbour on the south coast.
f: Blue Mountain coffee, grown on the eastern slopes, is among the most prized in the world.
Jamaica is the third-largest island in the Caribbean, after Cuba and Hispaniola.
Kingston Harbour, sheltered by a long sand spit called the Palisadoes, is one of the world's largest natural harbours.

q.q: What does the Taíno name Xaymaca mean?

Q2076337.t: Green mountains above the Atlantic's deepest trench
Q2076337.s: Puerto Rico is a nearly rectangular island, about 160 km long, with a spine of green mountains, the Cordillera Central, running from east to west. In the north-east, the peaks of El Yunque catch the trade winds and stay wrapped in rainforest and cloud. Off the north coast the seabed plunges into the Puerto Rico Trench, the deepest part of the Atlantic, more than 8 km down.
Q2076337.w: A rectangular green island east of Hispaniola, with mountains along its centre and the sprawl of San Juan on the north coast.
f: El Yunque is the only tropical rainforest in the US National Forest System.
Mosquito Bay on the nearby island of Vieques glows at night with bioluminescent plankton.
Cerro de Punta, the highest peak, reaches about 1,340 m.

q.q: What makes Mosquito Bay on Vieques famous?

Q128323.t: Three hills, a lake of tar and the steelpan
Q128323.s: Columbus named Trinidad in 1498 after the Holy Trinity, reportedly for three hills he saw on the horizon. The island is almost a rectangle, with a green mountain range along its north coast that continues the mountains of Venezuela across the water. The south-west holds a curiosity: Pitch Lake, the world's largest natural deposit of asphalt, a grey, wrinkled surface you can walk on.
Q128323.w: A roughly rectangular island off Venezuela's coast, with a green mountain ridge along the north and the Gulf of Paria to the west.
f: The steelpan, made from oil drums, was invented in Trinidad in the 20th century.
The scarlet ibis, Trinidad and Tobago's national bird, roosts in the Caroni Swamp.
At its closest, Trinidad is only about 11 km from Venezuela.

q.q: What fills Trinidad's famous Pitch Lake?

Q188489.t: An island with an inland sea at its heart
Q188489.s: Cape Breton hides a sea inside itself: Bras d'Or Lake, a branching body of salt water that fills much of the island's middle. In the north, the Cape Breton Highlands rise as a forested plateau that ends in steep cliffs above the Gulf of St Lawrence, blazing red and gold in autumn. Scottish settlers brought Gaelic here, and it still lives on in local music.
Q188489.w: A ragged island off Nova Scotia's north-eastern tip, with the branching blue Bras d'Or Lake in its centre and highlands in the north.
f: Since 1955 the Canso Causeway has linked the island to the Nova Scotia mainland.
In the 18th century the French built the Fortress of Louisbourg on its east coast.

q.q: What fills the centre of Cape Breton Island?

Q25277.t: The Caribbean's highest peaks and its lowest lake
Q25277.s: Hispaniola packs the extremes of the Caribbean into one island. Pico Duarte, at about 3,100 m, is the highest peak in the region, while Lake Enriquillo, a salty lake in a sunken valley, lies well below sea level. Between them run parallel mountain ranges separated by fertile valleys. The island is shared by Haiti in the west and the Dominican Republic in the east.
Q25277.w: A big mountainous island between Cuba and Puerto Rico; its western end splits into two long peninsulas like a lobster's open claws.
f: Santo Domingo, founded in the 1490s, is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the Americas.
Lake Enriquillo is home to American crocodiles and rhinoceros iguanas.
Hispaniola is the second-largest island in the Caribbean, after Cuba.

q.q: Which lake on Hispaniola lies below sea level?

Q586657.t: A long green crocodile stretched across the Caribbean
Q586657.s: Cubans call their island El Caimán, the crocodile, and its long, slender outline, more than 1,200 km from snout to tail, really does look like one. Much of it is gently rolling farmland of sugarcane, tobacco and royal palms, but the Sierra Maestra in the south-east rises to nearly 2,000 m. Along the north coast, strings of low cays sit in startlingly turquoise water.
Q586657.w: A very long, narrow island, mostly green and flat, with mountains in the far south-east and turquoise shallows off both coasts.
f: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, covering about 105,000 km².
In the west, the Viñales Valley is dotted with mogotes, steep-sided limestone hills rising from tobacco fields.
More than 4,000 smaller islands and cays surround the main island.

q.q: Which animal do Cubans see in the shape of their island?

Q215089.t: A long, thin island where men still call sharks
Q215089.s: New Ireland is one of the skinniest big islands anywhere: some 350 km long but in places only about 10 km wide, a green, mountainous ribbon curving across the Bismarck Sea. In a few villages, men still practise shark calling, luring sharks to their canoes with coconut-shell rattles. The island is also famous for malagan, intricate carved figures made for funeral ceremonies.
Q215089.w: A very long, narrow island curving from north-west to south-east, north-east of New Britain, with a mountain spine along its length.
f: Kavieng, the main town, sits at the island's north-western tip.
Malagan carvings from New Ireland are kept in major museums around the world.
Under German rule the island was called Neu-Mecklenburg.

q.q: Which traditional skill is New Ireland known for?

Q714573.t: A steep rainforest island at the Solomons' south-eastern end
Q714573.s: Makira rises from the sea as a long, steep ridge of rainforest, with few roads and small villages tucked along the coast. It lies at the south-eastern end of the main Solomon Islands chain, beyond Guadalcanal. Sailors of Mendaña's Spanish expedition named it San Cristóbal in 1568, and both names are still used. Its forests shelter birds found nowhere else.
Q714573.w: A long, narrow, forested island south-east of Guadalcanal, its ridges often in cloud.
f: Makira covers roughly 3,000 km² but has only a few short stretches of road.
The provincial capital, Kirakira, lies on its north coast.

q.q: What name did Spanish sailors give Makira in 1568?

Q713182.t: The long island where Europeans first met the Solomons
Q713182.s: In 1568 Álvaro de Mendaña's ships reached this island, the first of the Solomons seen by Europeans, and named it after Saint Elizabeth. Santa Isabel is long and slender, about 200 km from end to end, with a forested mountain spine and a coast broken into bays and small islands. Few people live here, and most of the island is still covered by rainforest.
Q713182.w: A long, slender, forested island running north-west to south-east between Choiseul and Guadalcanal, fringed with islets.
f: The Arnavon Islands, between Santa Isabel and Choiseul, are a major nesting site for hawksbill turtles.
The island's highest point, Mount Sasari, rises to about 1,200 m.

q.q: Which Solomon island did Mendaña's expedition reach first, in 1568?

Q618594.s: Malakula, Vanuatu's second-largest island, is a forested land of rugged hills, deep valleys and mangrove-lined bays. It is also one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth: roughly thirty languages are spoken here, some by only a few hundred people. In the interior live the Big Nambas and Small Nambas, peoples named after their traditional dress.
Q618594.w: A large green island with ragged, mangrove-lined coasts; Espiritu Santo lies to the north and volcanic Ambrym to the east.
f: Malakula covers about 2,000 km².
Lakatoro, on the east coast, is the main town and a provincial capital.

q.q: Roughly how many languages are spoken on Malakula?

Q713127.t: The busy heart of the Galápagos
Q713127.s: Round, green-topped Santa Cruz sits in the middle of the Galápagos and is the busiest island: Puerto Ayora, on its south coast, is the archipelago's largest town. The land rises gently to misty highlands, where giant tortoises wander through pastures and forests of tree daisies. Lonesome George, the last tortoise of his kind, lived out his life at the research station here.
Q713127.w: A round volcanic island in the centre of the Galápagos, green in its highlands, with the small airport island of Baltra off its north coast.
f: Twin pit craters called Los Gemelos open up in the highland forest.
The Charles Darwin Research Station at Puerto Ayora has worked to study and protect the islands since 1964.

q.q: Which famous tortoise lived at the station on Santa Cruz?

Q337519.t: A huge shield volcano with a black lava coast
Q337519.s: Savai'i is one broad shield volcano, rising gently from the reef to forested heights of nearly 1,860 m at Mount Silisili, the highest point in Samoa. Its north coast still carries a wide black scar: lava from the Matavanu eruption of 1905–11 flowed through villages down to the sea. The island's name is related to Hawaiki, the legendary homeland of the Polynesians.
Q337519.w: A big, rounded green island west of Upolu, a gentle volcanic dome with dark lava fields along its northern coast.
f: Savai'i is the largest island in Polynesia outside Hawaii and New Zealand.
At the Alofaaga blowholes on the south coast, waves shoot seawater high into the air.

q.q: What is the highest point in Samoa?

Q847008.t: The sacred island where Polynesian voyages began
Q847008.s: Raiatea shares one lagoon with its smaller neighbour Taha'a: two green, mountainous islands enclosed by a single ring of reef. For centuries this was the religious heart of eastern Polynesia, and from the great marae of Taputapuatea voyagers set out across the ocean. On the flat top of Mount Temehani grows the tiare apetahi, a white flower found nowhere else in the world.
Q847008.w: Two high green islands, Raiatea and Taha'a, inside one shared turquoise lagoon; Bora Bora lies to the north-west, Huahine to the east.
f: Taputapuatea became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017.
Raiatea's old name was Havai'i, echoed in the name of Hawai'i far to the north.

q.q: Which flower grows only on Raiatea's Mount Temehani?

Q937908.t: The island where Gauguin and Brel came to rest
Q937908.s: Hiva Oa is a rugged crescent of green ridges and plunging cliffs, with no reef to shelter its black-sand bays. Paul Gauguin spent his last years in the village of Atuona and was buried there in 1903; the Belgian singer Jacques Brel, who flew his own plane around the islands, lies in the same cemetery. At Puamau stand some of the largest stone tiki in Polynesia.
Q937908.w: A long, curving, mountainous island in the southern Marquesas, green ridges dropping steeply to the sea around a deep southern bay.
f: Mount Temetiu, the highest point, rises to about 1,200 m.
Hiva Oa is the second-largest of the Marquesas, after Nuku Hiva.

q.q: Which painter is buried on Hiva Oa?

Q21064.t: The Marquesan valleys that inspired Melville's 'Typee'
Q21064.s: In 1842 a young sailor named Herman Melville jumped ship in Taiohae Bay and spent weeks in a valley on this island; the adventure became his first book, Typee. Nuku Hiva is the largest of the Marquesas, a jagged mass of ridges around deep green valleys, with a high plateau in the middle. Its main village, Taiohae, is the administrative centre of the archipelago.
Q21064.w: The biggest island of the northern Marquesas: steep green ridges and deep bays around a broad, grassy central plateau.
f: Vaipo waterfall in the Hakaui valley drops about 350 m, one of the highest in French Polynesia.
Nuku Hiva covers about 340 km².

q.q: Which Melville book grew out of his stay on Nuku Hiva?

Q193331.t: Earth's largest coral atoll, early to greet the New Year
Q193331.s: Kiritimati is the biggest coral atoll in the world by land area, and from above it looks like a pale lobster claw filled with turquoise and green ponds. James Cook arrived here on Christmas Eve 1777, hence the name. Kiribati's Line Islands keep the world's earliest time zone, UTC+14, so every new year begins here before almost anywhere else on Earth.
Q193331.w: A large, pale, claw-shaped atoll just north of the equator, its lagoon broken into countless turquoise and green ponds.
f: Kiritimati is simply 'Christmas' written in the spelling of the Kiribati language.
Millions of seabirds, including huge colonies of sooty terns, nest on the atoll.

q.q: Why is Kiritimati also called Christmas Island?
x: Its palms look like fir trees
It was settled on Christmas Day

Q131347.t: Two old volcanoes, a city and the crater of Diamond Head
Q131347.s: Oahu is built from two old volcanoes, and you can still see them as two parallel mountain ranges: the Wai'anae in the west and the Ko'olau in the east, their cliffs fluted like organ pipes. Between them lies a green central plain. On the south coast, Honolulu spreads out beneath the crisp crater of Diamond Head, and at night the whole shoreline glitters.
Q131347.w: An island with two parallel mountain ranges; the city spreads along the south coast and ends at the round crater of Diamond Head.
f: About two-thirds of Hawaii's people live on Oahu.
The island's name is often translated as 'the gathering place'.
Diamond Head got its English name from sailors who mistook calcite crystals on its slopes for diamonds.

q.q: Which crater rises at the eastern end of Waikiki?

Q201026.t: The Garden Isle, carved by rain into canyons and cliffs
Q201026.s: Kauai is the oldest of the main Hawaiian islands, and millions of years of rain have carved it deeply. Near its centre, Mount Wai'ale'ale is one of the rainiest places on Earth; to the west, Waimea Canyon cuts a red-and-green gorge about 900 m deep. Along the north-west coast, the Nā Pali cliffs drop in sharp green pleats straight into the ocean.
Q201026.w: A round green island north-west of Oahu, with the red gash of Waimea Canyon in the west and the pleated Nā Pali cliffs.
f: In 1778 James Cook landed at Waimea on Kauai, the first recorded European visit to Hawaii.
Waimea Canyon is often called the Grand Canyon of the Pacific.
Mount Wai'ale'ale receives roughly 10 m of rain in an average year.

q.q: Who landed on Kauai in 1778?

Q327733.t: Fiji's quieter big island behind a great reef
Q327733.s: Vanua Levu, Fiji's second-largest island, is a long, irregular sweep of green hills, with sugarcane plains around Labasa in the north and palm-fringed bays in the south. Deep Natewa Bay almost cuts its eastern end in two. Off the north coast runs the Great Sea Reef, one of the longest barrier reefs in the world, a pale line drawn across the blue.
Q327733.w: A long, ragged green island north-east of Viti Levu, a deep bay biting into its eastern arm and a reef line to the north.
f: Vanua Levu covers about 5,600 km².
Its name means 'great land' in Fijian.
Savusavu, on the south coast, is a sheltered harbour popular with yachts.

q.q: What does the name Vanua Levu mean?

Q16635.t: Where America's day begins, on a limestone plateau
Q16635.s: Guam narrows at the waist like a footprint: the north is a flat limestone plateau ending in sheer cliffs above the sea, the south a jumble of volcanic hills with red earth. It is the largest and southernmost of the Mariana Islands. Because it lies so far west across the Pacific, its motto is 'Where America's Day Begins'.
Q16635.w: An elongated island narrowing in the middle: a flat, forested plateau in the north, hillier south, reefs all round.
f: Latte stones, pillars topped with stone half-spheres, once supported the houses of the Chamorro people.
Covering about 540 km², Guam is the largest island in Micronesia.

q.q: Guam is the largest island of which chain?

Q818749.t: A row of smoking volcanoes at the top of the Kurils
Q818749.s: Paramushir is essentially a row of volcanoes joined into one island, their cones capped with snow for much of the year. Chikurachki, the tallest at about 1,800 m, and Ebeko, close to the town of Severo-Kurilsk, regularly puff out ash. Just to the north lies little Shumshu, and beyond it Cape Lopatka, the southern tip of Kamchatka.
Q818749.w: A long, snowy volcanic island in the northern Kurils, its peaks in a line from north-east to south-west, with Kamchatka's tip just to the north.
f: Severo-Kurilsk, the island's only town, has a couple of thousand residents.
Covering about 2,000 km², Paramushir is one of the largest Kuril Islands.

q.q: Which peninsula's tip lies just north of Paramushir?

Q697278.t: Subtropical forests and a rabbit from another age
Q697278.s: Rugged and deeply green, Amami Ōshima lies in the chain of islands between Kyushu and Okinawa, its hills covered in dense subtropical forest and its bays edged with coral. These forests shelter the Amami rabbit, a dark, short-eared species regarded as a living fossil. Since 2021 the island has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage site. Its mud-dyed silk, Ōshima tsumugi, is among Japan's most prized fabrics.
Q697278.w: A rugged, deeply indented green island in the chain between Kyushu and Okinawa, with coral-fringed bays.
f: Amami rabbits live only on Amami Ōshima and neighbouring Tokunoshima.
Ōshima tsumugi threads are dyed with the tannin of a local tree and iron-rich mud.

q.q: Which rare animal lives only on Amami Ōshima and Tokunoshima?

Q1061195.t: Stepping stones from Mindanao to Borneo
Q1061195.s: Like stepping stones, the Sulu islands run south-west from the tip of Mindanao towards Borneo: Basilan, Jolo, Tawi-Tawi and hundreds of smaller ones, many ringed by turquoise shallows. For centuries this was the realm of the Sultanate of Sulu, a trading power dealing in pearls and sea cucumbers. Bajau sea people still live here in villages built on stilts over the water.
Q1061195.w: A long chain of green islands and reefs curving south-west from Mindanao's Zamboanga Peninsula towards Borneo.
f: The Sultanate of Sulu was founded in the 15th century.
The archipelago separates the Sulu Sea from the Celebes Sea.
Seaweed farming is one of the islands' main livelihoods.

q.q: Which two seas does the Sulu Archipelago separate?
x: The Philippine and South China seas

Q5813.t: Seven volcanic islands and Spain's highest peak
Q5813.s: Seven volcanic islands lie scattered off the coast of Africa, each with its own character: dark lava fields and craters on Lanzarote, pale dunes on Fuerteventura, deep green ravines on La Palma. In the middle of the chain, Tenerife's Teide rises to 3,715 m, the highest point in Spain, often poking above a sea of cloud. The islands are named after dogs, not birds.
Q5813.w: A west–east chain of islands off Morocco; Tenerife's volcanic cone, Teide, often stands above the clouds.
f: The Romans knew one island as Canaria, 'island of dogs'; the canary bird was later named after the islands.
Fuerteventura lies only about 100 km from the African coast.
Before the Spanish conquest the islands were home to the Guanches and related peoples.

q.q: Which peak on Tenerife is the highest point in Spain?

Q210907.t: Misty islands of the Haida on the edge of the continent
Q210907.s: Across the wide, stormy Hecate Strait from the British Columbia coast, Haida Gwaii rises as a triangle of dark-green islands. Some 150 of them, cloaked in rainforest of giant cedar and spruce, are often wrapped in mist. This is the homeland of the Haida, famed for their carved poles and ocean-going canoes. Unusual wildlife has earned the islands the nickname 'Galápagos of the North'.
Q210907.w: A triangular group of dark-forested islands well off the British Columbia coast, largest in the north, tapering to many small ones southward.
f: At SGang Gwaay, a UNESCO site, weathered Haida poles still stand in an abandoned village.
The islands were long known in English as the Queen Charlotte Islands; the official name changed in 2010.

q.q: Which strait separates Haida Gwaii from the mainland?

Q140510.t: A thousand forested islands along the Inside Passage
Q140510.s: Some 1,100 islands crowd the coast of south-east Alaska here, steep, dark with spruce and hemlock, and separated by narrow, fjord-like channels. Ships following the sheltered Inside Passage wind between them for hundreds of kilometres. On Baranof Island, Sitka was the capital of Russian America until Alaska was sold to the United States in 1867.
Q140510.w: A maze of steep, dark-green islands and narrow channels along the Alaska coast, with snowy mountains and glaciers on the mainland behind.
f: Most of the islands lie within the Tongass, the largest national forest in the United States.
The archipelago is named after the Russian tsar Alexander II.
These islands are the homelands of the Tlingit and Haida peoples.

q.q: Which town in the archipelago was the capital of Russian America?

Q306147.t: Wild islands off a crowded coast, home of a dwarf fox
Q306147.s: Just off one of the most crowded coastlines in America lie eight rugged, dry islands where the land looks almost untouched. Five of them form Channel Islands National Park; Santa Catalina, farther south, has a small resort town. Here lives the island fox, no bigger than a house cat, and in the Ice Age pygmy mammoths roamed Santa Rosa Island.
Q306147.w: A chain of brownish, cliff-edged islands off the coast between Santa Barbara and Los Angeles, the largest to the north-west.
f: Remains found on Santa Rosa Island, about 13,000 years old, are among the oldest human remains known in North America.
Santa Cruz is the largest island in California.

q.q: Which dwarf animal lived on Santa Rosa Island in the Ice Age?

Q179528.t: A green fan pressed against the desert
Q179528.s: Nowhere is the line between life and desert sharper: the Nile Delta spreads as a dense green fan, and at its edges the sand begins abruptly. North of Cairo the river splits into two branches, Rosetta to the west and Damietta to the east, and between them lies one of the most intensively farmed landscapes on Earth. At night the whole triangle glitters with towns and villages.
Q179528.w: A huge green triangle between yellow deserts, pointing south towards Cairo, its coast edged with shallow lagoons.
f: The ancient Greeks named it after the triangular letter delta.
The Rosetta Stone, the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs, was found in 1799 near the delta town of Rashid, or Rosetta.
Tens of millions of people live in the delta, though it covers only a small fraction of Egypt.

q.q: What are the Nile's two delta branches called?

Q2298744.t: A frozen fan of channels on the Laptev Sea
Q2298744.s: Before it reaches the Laptev Sea, the Lena splits into a vast fan of channels, islands and lakes about 400 km wide, the largest delta in the Arctic. In summer it is a mosaic of silver water and green-brown tundra; for the rest of the year it lies frozen and white. Tiksi, a port on the Northern Sea Route, stands just to the south-east.
Q2298744.w: A huge fan of silver channels and countless lakes spreading into the Laptev Sea, white and frozen for most of the year.
f: The delta covers about 32,000 km² and holds thousands of lakes.
Much of it is protected as part of the Ust-Lensky Nature Reserve.
The delta stays frozen for about seven to eight months of the year.

q.q: Into which sea does the Lena Delta spread?

Q1277365.t: A thirsty delta of creeks and mangroves
Q1277365.s: The Indus ends not in a lush fan but in a pale, braided maze of tidal creeks, mudflats and mangroves on the Arabian Sea coast. Dams and canals upstream now take most of its water, so the sea pushes salt far inland along the channels. Even so, its mangrove forests are among the largest in any arid climate, sheltering fish, shrimp and migrating birds.
Q1277365.w: A wide web of grey-brown tidal creeks and dark mangrove fringes on the coast south-east of Karachi.
f: The river's ancient name, Sindhu, is the root of the words India and Hindu.
The Indus rises in Tibet and flows more than 3,000 km to reach this coast.

q.q: Which big city lies just west of the Indus Delta?

Q1163759.t: The world's largest delta, woven from three rivers
Q1163759.s: Three great rivers, the Ganges, the Brahmaputra and the Meghna, braid together here into the largest delta on Earth. It is a green world of rice paddies and ponds, cut by wide, silty rivers whose sandbars shift with every monsoon. More than a hundred million people live on this low, fertile land, shared by Bangladesh and India, and its southern edge dissolves into the mangroves of the Sundarbans.
Q1163759.w: A vast flat green plain crossed by wide brown rivers and shifting sandbanks, fraying into dark mangrove islands along the Bay of Bengal.
f: The delta covers about 100,000 km², more than any other on Earth.
Its rivers carry around a billion tonnes of sediment to the sea each year.
Kolkata stands on the Hooghly, the delta's westernmost major branch.

q.q: Which river joins the Ganges to form this delta?

Q182561.t: A long, straight sandy shore on the Bay of Bengal
Q182561.s: The Coromandel Coast runs almost ruler-straight along the Bay of Bengal, a pale line of beach backed by lagoons, rice fields and palm groves. Its name probably comes from Chola Mandalam, 'realm of the Cholas', the dynasty that once ruled here. European traders followed: Chennai grew from an English fort, Puducherry was French and Tranquebar Danish.
Q182561.w: A long, smooth, sandy coastline running north–south, with Chennai's sprawl and the large Pulicat lagoon just north of it.
f: Unlike most of India, this coast gets much of its rain from the north-east monsoon, between October and December.
Pulicat Lake, north of Chennai, is India's second-largest brackish lagoon.
The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram, south of Chennai, has faced the sea since the 8th century.

q.q: Which dynasty probably gave the Coromandel Coast its name?

Q34709.t: A high salt desert striped by wind-carved ridges
Q34709.s: Ringed by the Kunlun, Qilian and Altyn-Tagh ranges, the Qaidam is a closed basin about 3 km above sea level, with no outlet to the ocean. Its floor is a pale desert of salt flats and briny lakes, some patched blue and green by evaporation ponds. In the north-west, wind has carved the ground into thousands of parallel ridges called yardangs, a pattern that looks like the surface of Mars.
Q34709.w: A vast, pale basin between snowy ranges, with white salt flats, coloured evaporation ponds and streaky wind-carved ridges.
f: Qarhan Salt Lake, in the basin, is China's largest source of potash.
The Qinghai–Tibet Railway crosses the basin at Golmud before climbing towards Lhasa.
Scientists study its yardangs and salt flats as a stand-in for Mars.

q.q: What are the Qaidam's wind-carved ridges called?

Q2155625.t: Flat irrigated plains between two rivers
Q2155625.s: The Riverina is flat, very flat: towards the west, the Hay Plain is often called one of the flattest places on Earth. Rivers give it life, the Murray along the south and the Murrumbidgee through the middle, and irrigation turns parts of the dry plain into a geometric grid of rice paddies, orchards and vineyards. Elsewhere, sheep and wheat stretch to a bare horizon.
Q2155625.w: Wide flat plains, geometric green irrigated fields along winding rivers lined with red gums, dry brown land beyond.
f: Australia's rice industry is centred on the Riverina's irrigation areas around Leeton and Griffith.
Wagga Wagga, on the Murrumbidgee, is the region's largest city.
The name comes from 'riverine', meaning land beside rivers.

q.q: Which crop, surprising in dry Australia, grows here in paddies?

Q1052359.t: The Silk Road's green corridor between snow and sand
Q1052359.s: Snowy peaks of the Qilian Shan on one side, stony desert on the other, and between them a long, narrow belt of green oases: this is the Hexi Corridor, the natural route of the Silk Road from China towards Central Asia. Meltwater rivers from the mountains feed a chain of oasis towns such as Wuwei, Zhangye and Jiuquan. At Jiayuguan the Ming Great Wall reached its western end.
Q1052359.w: A long green strip of fields between a snow-capped range to the south-west and pale desert to the north-east.
f: Hexi means 'west of the river': the corridor lies west of the Yellow River.
The corridor stretches for roughly 1,000 km.
Near Zhangye, the Danxia landforms are banded in red, orange and yellow.

q.q: Which fortress marks the western end of the Ming Great Wall?

Q673287.t: Where the Yangtze squeezes between limestone walls
Q673287.s: For about 200 km the Yangtze cuts through the Wu Mountains in three narrow gorges, Qutang, Wu and Xiling, with limestone walls rising hundreds of metres above the water. From the air the river becomes a thin, winding band of grey-green between folded, forested ridges. Near the eastern end, the Three Gorges Dam has turned the river upstream into a reservoir some 600 km long.
Q673287.w: A narrow, twisting river threading between steep, forested ridges, between Chongqing and Yichang.
f: Kuimen, the gateway of Qutang Gorge, appears on the back of the 10-yuan banknote.
The Three Gorges Dam is the world's largest hydroelectric power station by installed capacity.

q.q: Which Chinese banknote shows Kuimen, the gateway of Qutang Gorge?

Q19742.t: The deepest canyon on Earth, bent around a giant peak
Q19742.s: Here the Yarlung Tsangpo, Tibet's great river, makes a hairpin turn around Namcha Barwa, a 7,782 m peak, and plunges into the deepest canyon on Earth. Between that summit and Gyala Peri across the gorge, the canyon is more than 5 km deep. Below the bend the river turns south towards the plains of Assam, where it becomes the Brahmaputra.
Q19742.w: A sharp hairpin of river gorge wrapped around a huge, glaciated peak, Namcha Barwa, at the eastern end of the Himalaya.
f: The canyon is about 500 km long, longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.
Namcha Barwa, guarding the bend, was first climbed only in 1992.
A waterfall hidden deep in the gorge was reached by explorers only in the late 1990s.

q.q: What does the Yarlung Tsangpo become downstream?

Q1031793.t: Chile's long garden between two mountain walls
Q1031793.s: Squeezed between the high Andes to the east and the lower Coastal Range to the west, the Central Valley runs for hundreds of kilometres down the middle of Chile. It is the country's farm and orchard, with vineyards in the north giving way to wheat, pastures and pine plantations farther south. Around Temuco, snow-capped volcanoes such as Llaima and Villarrica stand guard along its eastern edge.
Q1031793.w: A long, flat, farmed lowland running north–south between the white Andes and a lower green coastal range, with volcanic cones to the east.
f: Most Chileans live in the Central Valley, which also holds Santiago.
Its northern half, with a Mediterranean-like climate, is one of South America's great wine regions.
Villarrica, rising near the valley's edge south-east of Temuco, is one of Chile's most active volcanoes.

q.q: Which range borders Chile's Central Valley on the west?

Q27026.t: America's great orchard, flat as a table
Q27026.s: Between the Sierra Nevada and the Coast Ranges lies a flat valley some 700 km long, one of the most productive farming regions on Earth. It is an endless grid of orchards, vineyards and fields, crossed by canals carrying water south. Near its southern end lies the bed of Tulare Lake, once the largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi, now farmland that floods only in very wet years.
Q27026.w: A vast flat valley chequered with green and brown fields, the snowy Sierra Nevada to the east and lower Coast Ranges to the west.
f: The valley grows about a quarter of the food produced in the United States.
Pumping groundwater has made parts of the valley floor sink by several metres.
In winter a dense, low 'tule fog' can fill the valley for days.

q.q: Which lake once filled part of the southern Central Valley?

Q140948.t: Ice-capped islands and a volcano you can sail into
Q140948.s: Glacier-covered and ringed by dark cliffs, the South Shetlands form a long chain off the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula. Deception Island is the strangest: a ring-shaped volcano whose flooded crater ships enter through a narrow gap called Neptune's Bellows. King George Island hosts more research stations than almost anywhere else in Antarctica, run by many different countries.
Q140948.w: A chain of white, glacier-capped islands north of the Antarctic Peninsula; Deception Island's ring shape lies on the south side of the chain.
f: William Smith sighted the islands in 1819 after being blown south while rounding Cape Horn.
Visitors sometimes bathe in volcanically warmed water on Deception Island's beaches.

q.q: How do ships enter Deception Island's flooded crater?

Q192188.t: Remote atolls around the largest atoll structure on Earth
Q192188.s: In the middle of the Indian Ocean, some 60 low coral islands are scattered across the Chagos atolls. The Great Chagos Bank is the largest atoll structure in the world, a vast, mostly submerged ring with only a few specks of land on its rim. The reefs here are among the most pristine on Earth, and much of the surrounding ocean has been protected as a marine reserve.
Q192188.w: Tiny low islands and pale reef rings with turquoise lagoons, far out in deep blue ocean south of the Maldives.
f: The Great Chagos Bank covers about 18,000 km², yet its islands add up to only a few square kilometres.
The Chagos lie at the southern end of a line of atolls that also includes the Maldives and the Laccadives.

q.q: Which chain of atolls lies north of the Chagos?

Q118223.t: A lonely arc of smoking volcanoes in the Southern Ocean
Q118223.s: Far out in the stormy Southern Ocean, a curved chain of volcanic islands rises from the sea, most of them capped with ice and several still active. James Cook sighted them in 1775 and named them after the Earl of Sandwich. Nobody lives here, but Zavodovski Island hosts one of the largest penguin colonies on Earth, with chinstrap penguins in the hundreds of thousands.
Q118223.w: A north–south arc of small, white, cone-shaped islands in open ocean, some trailing plumes of steam.
f: East of the islands, the South Sandwich Trench plunges more than 8 km.
Mount Belinda, the volcano on Montagu Island, erupted through its ice cap in the early 2000s.

q.q: Who named the South Sandwich Islands in 1775?

Q1266371.t: A 'hundred thousand islands' that add up to 32 km²
Q1266371.s: The name Lakshadweep means 'a hundred thousand islands', yet there are only 36, and together they cover about 32 km². They are delicate rings of turquoise lagoon and white sand, each with a thin green strip of coconut palms along its eastern edge. The islands lie 200–400 km off the coast of Kerala, and only ten of them are inhabited.
Q1266371.w: Scattered turquoise lagoons with thin green islets, far out in the Arabian Sea west of India's south-western coast.
f: Minicoy, the southernmost island, speaks a language close to that of the Maldives.
Coconuts and tuna fishing are the mainstays of island life.

q.q: What does the name Lakshadweep mean?

Q25389.t: A low green peninsula where two seas collide
Q25389.s: Jutland is the only part of Denmark joined to mainland Europe: a low peninsula of fields, heath and dunes pointing north towards Norway. At its tip, at Skagen, the Skagerrak and the Kattegat meet in a line of clashing waves. The long Limfjord cuts right across the north from sea to sea, and on the south-west coast the Wadden Sea's tidal flats appear and vanish twice a day.
Q25389.w: A long, low peninsula of green and brown fields between the North Sea and the Kattegat, crossed in the north by the winding Limfjord.
f: Råbjerg Mile, near Skagen, is a migrating sand dune that moves up to about 15 m a year.
Lego was born in Billund, in the middle of Jutland.
The peninsula continues south into Germany as Schleswig-Holstein.

q.q: Which two seas meet at Skagen, Jutland's northern tip?

Q849318.t: Volcanic islands where giant mantas meet divers
Q849318.s: Four small volcanic islands lie far out in the Pacific, several hundred kilometres south-west of the tip of Baja California. Socorro is the largest, its volcano rising to about 1,050 m; on San Benedicto, a whole new volcano, Bárcena, appeared in 1952. The surrounding waters are famous for giant manta rays, sharks and humpback whales.
Q849318.w: A few small, dark volcanic islands scattered far apart in the open Pacific, south of Baja California.
f: The islands have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2016.
Since 2017 the waters around them have formed one of the largest fully protected marine reserves in North America.
They are named after a Spanish viceroy of New Spain, the Count of Revillagigedo.

q.q: Which volcano appeared on San Benedicto Island in 1952?

Q169532.t: England's granite toe, dipped in the Atlantic
Q169532.s: Here England simply runs out: granite cliffs drop into the Atlantic at the westernmost point of its mainland.
